All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) is a map \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(f(u)f(v)\in E(H)\) whenever \(uv\in E(G)\); the map need not be injective.

For a real number \(c\in[0,1]\), consider the following property: there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\), every graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), and in which every vertex has at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\). The graph \(H_c\) may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\) or \(G\).

What is the exact infimum of the numbers \(c\in[0,1]\) having this property?

\[
\boxed{\frac15}
\]

The relevant result is the **sharp odd-girth homomorphism-threshold theorem**. Its \(7\)-odd-girth case has the following two parts:

* For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a finite graph \(F_\varepsilon\) of odd girth at least \(7\) such that every graph \(G\) of odd girth at least \(7\) with
  \[
  \delta(G)\ge \left(\frac15+\varepsilon\right)|V(G)|
  \]
  admits a homomorphism to \(F_\varepsilon\).
* For every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every finite triangle-free graph \(H\), there is a graph \(G\) of odd girth at least \(7\) such that
  \[
  \delta(G)\ge \left(\frac15-\varepsilon\right)|V(G)|
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad G\nrightarrow H.
  \]
  Importantly, this lower-bound statement allows the proposed target \(H\) to contain \(5\)-cycles.

Here, having odd girth at least \(7\) is exactly the condition of containing neither a \(3\)-cycle nor a \(5\)-cycle.

If \(c>1/5\), apply the first part with \(\varepsilon=c-1/5\). The resulting \(F_\varepsilon\) is, in particular, triangle-free, so it can serve as \(H_c\).

Conversely, let \(c<1/5\) and suppose a finite triangle-free target \(H_c\) existed. Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(1/5-\varepsilon>c\). The second part gives a graph satisfying all the hypotheses in the question, with minimum degree greater than \(c|V(G)|\), but with no homomorphism to \(H_c\), a contradiction.

Thus every \(c>1/5\) works and every \(c<1/5\) fails. Whether the endpoint itself works is unnecessary for determining the infimum.

My previous answer incorrectly imposed a stronger restriction on the target: the target here may contain \(5\)-cycles.

The relevant **regularity-based odd-girth reduction result** is:

> For every \(d>0\), there is an integer \(M(d)\) such that every graph \(G\) with
> \[
> \delta(G)\ge d|V(G)|
> \]
> and containing neither a triangle nor a pentagon admits a homomorphism to a triangle-free graph with at most \(M(d)\) vertices.

The exceptional vertices in a regularity partition must receive additional neighborhood labels; simply mapping vertices to regularity clusters is insufficient. The absence of pentagons is what prevents these extra labels from creating triangles in the target. The target need not remain pentagon-free.

To obtain one universal target for a fixed \(d>0\), take the disjoint union of all triangle-free graphs on at most \(M(d)\) vertices, up to isomorphism. This is a finite triangle-free graph, and every eligible \(G\) maps into one of its components.

Thus **every \(c>0\) has the stated property**. Since the permitted values lie in \([0,1]\), their infimum is \(0\).

import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
from itertools import combinations
from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix
m,r,L=5,2,1
sets=list(map(frozenset,combinations(range(m),r)))
Q=nx.Graph();Q.add_nodes_from(range(len(sets)))
Q.add_edges_from((u,v) for u,v in combinations(Q.nodes,2) if sets[u].isdisjoint(sets[v]))
F=nx.Graph();F.add_nodes_from(Q);C=[list(Q),[],[]];phi={u:sets[u] for u in Q}
for u,v in Q.edges:
 a=('a',u,v);b=('b',u,v)
 C[1].append(a);C[2].append(b)
 F.add_edges_from([(u,a),(a,b),(b,v)])
 phi[a]=sets[v];phi[b]=sets[u]
violations=[]
for u in F:
 reach={u}
 for _ in range(3):reach={w for v in reach for w in F[v]}
 for v in reach:
  if not phi[u].isdisjoint(phi[v]):violations.append((u,v))
print('Failure of three-walk label disjointness:',len(violations))
G=F.copy()
for j in range(3):
 B=[('B',j,k) for k in range(r*L)]
 for i in range(m):
  A=[('A',j,i,k) for k in range(L)]
  G.add_edges_from((a,b) for a in A for b in B)
  G.add_edges_from((v,a) for v in C[j] if i in phi[v] for a in A)
A=csr_matrix(nx.to_scipy_sparse_array(G,dtype=np.int64)); A2=A@A;A3=A2@A
print('Triangle closed walks:',A.multiply(A2).sum())
print('Length-five closed walks:',A2.multiply(A3).sum())
print('F vertices:',len(F),'G vertices:',len(G),'minimum degree:',min(dict(G.degree()).values()))
print('Asymptotic min-degree proportion for fixed m,r:',r/(3*(m+r)))
print('As m/r tends to 2, proportion tends to',1/9)

The correct infimum is
\[
\boxed{\frac19}.
\]
The distinction between a triangle-free target and a target that is also pentagon-free matters here. Below are matching bounds.

## 1. Lower bound: every \(c<1/9\) fails

For a triangle-free graph \(X\), let \(X^{[3]}\) join two vertices whenever there is a walk of length three between them. If \(X\to H\) and \(H\) is triangle-free, then
\[
\chi(X^{[3]})\le |V(H)|.
\tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the endpoints of a three-edge walk cannot have the same image: that would give a closed three-edge walk in \(H\).

We construct triangle- and pentagon-free graphs of minimum-degree proportion approaching \(1/9\), with unbounded \(\chi(X^{[3]})\).

Take the Kneser graph
\[
Q=KG(m,r),\qquad m=2r+s.
\]
Its vertices are the \(r\)-subsets of \([m]\), with disjoint sets adjacent, and the Kneser chromatic-number theorem gives
\[
\chi(Q)=s+2.
\]

Replace each edge \(ST\) of \(Q\) by a three-edge path
\[
S-a_{ST}-b_{ST}-T,
\]
obtaining \(F\). Its vertices have three independent classes:
\[
C_0=V(Q),\qquad C_1=\{a_{ST}\},\qquad C_2=\{b_{ST}\}.
\]
Give each vertex an \(r\)-subset label by
\[
\ell(S)=S,\qquad \ell(a_{ST})=T,\qquad \ell(b_{ST})=S.
\]
A useful feature of this labeling is:

> The endpoints of every three-edge walk in \(F\) have disjoint labels.

This follows directly by examining a walk along the subdivided edges.

For each \(j\in\{0,1,2\}\), add:
* sets \(A_{j,i}\) of size \(L\), for \(i\in[m]\);
* a set \(B_j\) of size \(rL\);
* all edges between \(B_j\) and \(\bigcup_i A_{j,i}\).

For \(x\in C_j\), join \(x\) to every vertex of \(A_{j,i}\) whenever \(i\in\ell(x)\). Call the resulting graph \(G\).

Then
\[
|V(G)|=|V(F)|+3(m+r)L,\qquad \delta(G)\ge rL.
\tag{2}
\]

### Why there are no triangles or pentagons

The added bulk graphs are bipartite. A pentagon using a vertex of \(B_j\) would force an edge of \(F\) inside \(C_j\), which is impossible.

A pentagon using exactly one added \(A\)-vertex would give a three-edge path in \(F\) whose endpoint labels share an element, contrary to the labeling property. A pentagon using two \(A\)-vertices would again force an edge inside one \(C_j\). Triangles are excluded similarly. Finally, \(F\) itself has girth at least nine.

Moreover, the original vertices \(V(Q)\) induce a copy of \(Q\) in \(G^{[3]}\). Hence
\[
\chi(G^{[3]})\ge s+2.
\tag{3}
\]

Given any finite triangle-free \(H\) and any \(c<1/9\), first choose \(s\) with \(s+2>|V(H)|\), then choose \(r\) sufficiently large that
\[
\frac{r}{3(m+r)}
=\frac{r}{3(3r+s)}>c.
\]
Finally choose \(L\) large. Equation (2) gives \(\delta(G)\ge c|V(G)|\), while (1) and (3) show \(G\nrightarrow H\).

Thus every \(c<1/9\) fails.

## 2. Upper bound: every \(c>1/9\) works

Here is the regularity argument; all error terms below can be made arbitrarily small.

Apply the degree-form regularity lemma to \(G\). It gives boundedly many equal-sized clusters \(V_1,\dots,V_k\), covering all but \(o(n)\) vertices, and a reduced graph \(R\) satisfying
\[
\delta(R)\ge (c-o(1))k.
\tag{4}
\]
Each reduced edge represents a regular pair of positive density.

Fix a small threshold \(\eta\), and define
\[
S(v)=\{i:|N_G(v)\cap V_i|\ge\eta |V_i|\}.
\]
Regularity and the exclusion of triangles and pentagons give three useful rules:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&S(v)\text{ is independent in }R; \tag{5}\\
&uv\in E(G)\Longrightarrow
S(u)\cap S(v)=\varnothing,\quad
N_R(S(u))\cap N_R(S(v))=\varnothing; \tag{6}\\
&u-w-v\text{ is a two-edge walk}
\Longrightarrow E_R(S(u),S(v))=\varnothing. \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]
For example, a common reduced neighbor in (6) supplies a four-edge walk from \(u\) to \(v\), which together with \(uv\) gives a forbidden closed five-edge walk. The other rules follow in the same way.

Partition the vertices initially as follows.

* A vertex is **safe** if it has more than half of some cluster as neighbors; assign it to the first such cluster.
* Partition the remaining, **hard**, vertices according to their signature \(S(v)\).

Each safe class contains no endpoints of a three-edge walk: two vertices in it have a common neighbor, which would close such a walk into a forbidden five-edge walk.

For a hard vertex, every cluster contributes at most half its vertices to its neighborhood. Consequently,
\[
|S(v)|\ge (2c-o(1))k.
\tag{8}
\]
All initial classes are independent; for hard classes this follows from (6).

Now refine each initial class by recording the set of initial classes containing a neighbor. Form the quotient graph \(T\) on the resulting classes. Its order is bounded in terms of \(c\), and the quotient map is a homomorphism.

We claim that \(T\) is triangle-free. Suppose it had a triangle.

If one of its initial classes were safe, the other two refined classes would supply a three-edge walk with both endpoints in that safe class—a contradiction. Thus all three initial classes are hard; write their signatures as \(S_1,S_2,S_3\).

By (6), the \(S_i\) are pairwise disjoint, as are their reduced neighborhoods. The recorded neighbor-class information also supplies two-edge walks between every pair of initial classes. By (7), there are no reduced edges between distinct \(S_i\); by (5), none occur within an \(S_i\). Therefore the six sets
\[
S_1,S_2,S_3,\ N_R(S_1),N_R(S_2),N_R(S_3)
\]
are pairwise disjoint.

Using (4) and (8),
\[
k\ge\sum_{i=1}^{3}\bigl(|S_i|+|N_R(S_i)|\bigr)
\ge (9c-o(1))k,
\]
which is impossible when \(c>1/9\) and the regularity parameters are sufficiently small.

Thus \(T\) is triangle-free and has bounded order. Taking the disjoint union of all possible triangle-free targets up to that order gives one finite target depending only on \(c\).

Hence every \(c>1/9\) works, and every \(c<1/9\) fails, proving the stated infimum.

Now refine each initial class by recording the set of initial classes containing a neighbor. Form the quotient graph \(T\) on the resulting classes. Its order is bounded in terms of \(c\), and the quotient map is a homomorphism.

We claim that \(T\) is triangle-free. Suppose it had a triangle.

If one of its initial classes were safe, the other two refined classes would supply a three-edge walk with both endpoints in that safe class—a contradiction. Thus all three initial classes are hard; write their signatures as \(S_1,S_2,S_3\).

By (6), the \(S_i\) are pairwise disjoint, as are their reduced neighborhoods. The recorded neighbor-class information also supplies two-edge walks between every pair of initial classes. By (7), there are no reduced edges between distinct \(S_i\); by (5), none occur within an \(S_i\). Therefore the six sets
\[
S_1,S_2,S_3,\ N_R(S_1),N_R(S_2),N_R(S_3)
\]
are pairwise disjoint.

Using (4) and (8),
\[
k\ge\sum_{i=1}^{3}\bigl(|S_i|+|N_R(S_i)|\bigr)
\ge (9c-o(1))k,
\]
which is impossible when \(c>1/9\) and the regularity parameters are sufficiently small.

Thus \(T\) is triangle-free and has bounded order. Taking the disjoint union of all possible triangle-free targets up to that order gives one finite target depending only on \(c\).

Hence every \(c>1/9\) works, and every \(c<1/9\) fails, proving the stated infimum.

## Upper bound: every \(c>1/9\) works

Define \(J\) on \(V(G)\) by joining distinct vertices whenever a \(G\)-walk of length \(1\) or \(3\) connects them. The main task is to bound \(\chi(J)\) solely in terms of \(c\).

A \(q\)-coloring \(f\) of \(J\) gives an explicit triangle-free target \(W_q\). Its vertices are
\[
(i,S),\qquad i\in[q],\quad S\subseteq[q]\setminus\{i\},
\]
with adjacency defined by
\[
(i,S)\sim(j,T)\iff i\in T,\ j\in S,\ S\cap T=\varnothing.
\]
Map \(x\) to \((f(x),f(N_G(x)))\). For a \(G\)-edge \(xy\), the neighbor-color sets are disjoint because every neighbor of \(x\) and neighbor of \(y\) are connected by a three-edge walk. A triangle in \(W_q\) would force the first coordinate of its third vertex into the disjoint sets attached to its first two vertices. Thus \(W_q\) is triangle-free and has at most \(q2^{q-1}\) vertices.

### Regularity profiles and the nine-part obstruction

Set
\[
t=(9c-1)/1000,\qquad \varepsilon=t^2.
\]
Apply equitable regularity, then discard clusters with too many irregular partners. With sufficiently many initial clusters, the retained reduced graph \(R\), on \(k\) equal clusters, satisfies
\[
\delta(R)\ge(c-6t)k.
\]
Its edges represent regular pairs of density at least \(t\).

For each vertex \(v\), define its support \(S_v\) as the clusters in which \(v\) has at least \(t\) times the cluster size neighbors. At most \(4tn\) neighbors lie outside its support. Consequently, any profile class containing a \(J\)-edge has support size at least
\[
2(c-4t)k.
\]
Indeed, endpoints of a \(J\)-edge have disjoint \(G\)-neighborhoods: a common neighbor would produce a triangle or a \(5\)-cycle.

Regular-pair connector arguments establish:

1. Each \(S_v\) is independent in \(R\).
2. If \(xy\in E(G)\), then \(N_R(S_x)\cap N_R(S_y)=\varnothing\).
3. If \(x,z,y\) is a two-edge walk, no \(R\)-edge joins \(S_x\) to \(S_y\).

These follow by embedding respectively a triangle or a \(5\)-cycle if the stated restriction fails.

There are at most \(M=2^k\) profiles. If a profile class \(p\) had chromatic number greater than \(2^{M^2}\) in \(J\), color each of its \(J\)-edges by the ordered profiles \((q,r)\) of a chosen witness
\[
x-a-b-y.
\]
One edge-color subgraph must be nonbipartite. Any orientation of a nonbipartite graph contains a directed two-edge path, yielding a witness chain
\[
p-q-r-p-q-r-p.
\]
Thus all three profiles contain \(J\)-edges, and the chain supplies every required edge and two-edge relation between their types.

The connector restrictions imply that the following six sets are pairwise disjoint:
\[
S_p,S_q,S_r,\quad N_R(S_p),N_R(S_q),N_R(S_r).
\]
The first three each have size at least \(2(c-4t)k\); the latter three each have size at least \((c-6t)k\). Hence
\[
k\ge(9c-42t)k>k,
\]
a contradiction. Therefore
\[
\chi(J)\le M\,2^{M^2},
\]
uniformly in \(n\). Small graphs excluded by regularity’s size requirements are handled by adding finitely many triangle-free components to the target.

They also supplied an energy-increment proof of regularity: exceptional vertices remain singleton partition parts, so equitization inside refined atoms loses no energy. This closes the standard-lemma dependency.

## Lower bound: every \(c<1/9\) fails

Fix a finite triangle-free \(H\), and put \(h=\max(1,|V(H)|)\).

Use the shift graph \(F=S(N,k)\), where \(k\ge3\) is odd: vertices are increasing \(k\)-tuples, with edges between consecutive overlapping tuples from an increasing \((k+1)\)-tuple.

Two elementary facts supply the construction:

- A \(q\)-coloring of \(S(N,j)\) gives a \(2^q\)-coloring of \(S(N,j-1)\), by assigning each tuple the set of colors of its extensions. Iterating down to \(S(N,1)=K_N\) proves \(\chi(F)>h\) for sufficiently large \(N\).
- For each permutation \(\pi\), take tuples whose \(\pi\)-largest element occupies an even position. This is independent. Each tuple belongs to exactly
  \[
  p=\frac{(k-1)N!}{2k}
  \]
  of these \(m=N!\) independent sets. Write its permutation-label set as \(I_u\); adjacent labels have disjoint sets.

Replace every oriented edge \(u\to v\) by \(u-a_{uv}-b_{uv}-v\), obtaining \(X\). Give these vertices types \(0,1,2\) and labels \(u,u,v\). Same-type endpoints of any three-edge \(X\)-walk have adjacent labels.

Add three disjoint bicliques \(K_{mL,pL}\). In biclique \(i\), index the large side by permutations and \(L\) copies. Attach each type-\(i\) vertex with label \(u\) to the copies indexed by \(I_u\). Then
\[
n=|X|+3(m+p)L,\qquad \delta(G)\ge pL,
\]
and
\[
\frac{p}{3(m+p)}=\frac{k-1}{3(3k-1)}\longrightarrow\frac19.
\]
Choose \(k\), then \(L\), to obtain \(\delta(G)\ge cn\).

A complete cycle classification excludes triangles and \(5\)-cycles: \(X\) has girth at least nine; biclique-side vertices cannot participate; and remaining mixed \(5\)-cycles would require either a same-type \(X\)-edge or intersecting label sets of adjacent labels.

Finally, \(G\to H\) would properly color \(F\) with at most \(h\) colors: identifying endpoints of a subdivided edge would create a closed three-edge walk in \(H\), hence a triangle. Contradiction.
